name: David Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt, basically. I run a dozer at the bauxite mine, clearing the topsoil ahead of the diggers and shaping the dumps so they don't slump in the rain. Two and a half years in, before that I drove a delivery truck for a building supplies yard for fifteen years. I keep a little notebook in the cab where I write down every new thing the trainer tells me, because I'm still the slowest on the crew at reading the grade.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the quiet, honestly, me and the machine and the radio, and watching a messy slope turn into a neat one by lunchtime. Hard is the money still being tight. Hanna works at the nursing home, we've got Freya and Jonas, and after the mortgage and the car there's maybe forty left in a good fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and get on with it. I'm not one to post much. If someone at work brought it up, I'd say the tools are handy for some things and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means not much for me, which is fine. I use one of those AI apps now and then to sort out our budget and Hanna's rosters, so it's useful, but it was never going to drive my dozer. The bigger worry for me has always been the bauxite price, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and try to get my grading good enough for the next pay step, which is about a year away. I'd keep using the app for the budget. And I'd try to get the car paid off so there's more room each fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same old, and same old is all right by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bauxite price worries you more. How so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the price dropped three years before I started, they put half the contractors off in one week. Nobody needed a robot for that. So I've always thought the real boss is the price on the screen in some office somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the next pay step mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About sixty more a fortnight after tax. That's Jonas's football boots without a fight, or a bit into savings. It sounds small but it's the difference between tight and okay.

S0.say: He'd say that's that and get on with it, describing AI tools as handy for some things. He rarely posts online.
S0.think: He thinks it means little for him, since an AI app helps with budgets but was never going to drive his dozer. His real long-standing worry is the bauxite price.
S0.do: Keeps working towards the next pay step on grading, about a year away. Keeps using the budgeting app and works to pay off the car to free up money.
S0.feel: Calm; same old is all right by him.
S0.quote: So I've always thought the real boss is the price on the screen in some office somewhere.
S0.fieldNote: David is even-tempered and practical, and sees commodity prices as the real threat to his job. He already uses AI for household tasks without fuss. His goals are small and concrete, like the next pay step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people adapted to the computer and the mobile phone, and we'll adapt to this. The company should give people a fair chance at the new jobs. I wouldn't be shouting about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think dozers are a bit later to go than the haul trucks, because the ground's always different. That buys me some time. But I'm junior, and if the crew shrinks, the junior guys go first, so I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other crews do and follow the ones who seem to be landing on their feet. If the company offered training on the remote dozers, I'd sign up once I'd seen a couple of guys do it. Meanwhile I'd try to put away twenty a week, and I'd use the AI app to look up what the remote dozer course involves before I put my hand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. Like a noise in the engine you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until a couple of guys had done it. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first lot are the guinea pigs. When the yard brought in the new scanning system, the first guys spent six months fixing its mistakes. I'd rather go second and get the version that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hanna think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hanna would say go now, she's braver than me. She'd probably be right. But she'd also be the one pointing out we can't afford for me to drop shifts for a course.

S1.say: He'd say people adapted to computers and phones and will adapt to this, and the company should give workers a fair chance at new jobs, without making a fuss either way.
S1.think: He thinks dozers will be automated later than haul trucks because ground conditions vary, which buys him time. But as a junior operator he'd watch closely.
S1.do: Watches which crews land on their feet and signs up for remote dozer training once a couple of colleagues have done it. Saves twenty a week and uses the AI app to research the course first.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an engine noise he can't place yet.
S1.quote: I'd rather go second and get the version that works.
S1.fieldNote: David's steady approach is deliberate: he prefers to follow proven paths after seeing others go first. He gives a reasoned case for why dozers may last longer. His partner is the bolder one, and he acknowledges it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is way too fast and the government needs a plan, and quickly. I'm not a big government man, but nobody else can move that fast. I'd still say it calmly, there's no point shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it means my job goes, maybe in the first year, because if robots can do everything then the dozer's no different. Hanna's nursing home might hold on a bit longer, people want a person when they're old. But we'd be living on one small wage with a mortgage and almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go through the budget with the app that first weekend and cut everything we can. I'd look hard at moving to the city where Hanna's sister lives, because there'd at least be more of everything there, including care jobs for Hanna. I'd ask the bank early about lowering the payments, before we're behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at two in the morning with the notebook doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving mean for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freya's fourteen, she'd hate us for a year, her friends are her whole life. Jonas would be fine as long as there's a football team. I'd feel terrible about Freya, but a roof matters more than a school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for work in the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I'd take anything with a paycheque: driving, warehouse, helping Hanna's sister in her cleaning business. If the robots are doing all that too, then I'm not sure what the city gives me except more people in the same boat.

S2.say: He'd say it's far too fast and the government needs a plan quickly, while admitting he's not usually a big-government person. He'd say it calmly.
S2.think: He thinks his dozer job goes, perhaps in the first year. Hanna's care work might last longer, leaving them on one small wage with a mortgage and almost no savings.
S2.do: Cuts every possible cost using the budgeting app in the first weekend. Looks seriously at moving to the city near Hanna's sister and asks the bank early about lowering repayments.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at two in the morning doing sums in his notebook.
S2.quote: I'd feel terrible about Freya, but a roof matters more than a school.
S2.fieldNote: David stays calm in tone even when describing an alarming situation. He looks to his partner's care work as the more durable income and considers a move. He admits a move may not help if robots are doing city jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now. The company and the government both have a part to play. I'd tell the younger guys on the crew not to sit around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I could get through a proper course in that time, maybe a heavy diesel mechanic's ticket. The robots still need fixing, at least for a while. But I'd be fifty with a new trade, competing with twenty-five-year-olds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the first year closely and once it's clear which way things are going, I'd start the mechanic's course part-time in year two. We'd save what we can and pay off the car early. I'd use the AI app to help with the theory, because my reading's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch for a year first. Is that time you can afford?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question, isn't it. In five years, a year of watching is a fifth of it gone. Maybe I'd start sooner, maybe that's the lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut to make the course possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fishing trip with my brother, which we do every autumn. Maybe the second car. Hanna would pick up an extra shift, which I'd hate, because she's already worn out.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now, with company and government both playing a part, and he'd urge younger crewmates to act.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to earn a heavy diesel mechanic's ticket, since robots still need fixing for a while. But he'd be fifty competing with much younger people.
S3.do: Watches the first year, then starts a part-time mechanic's course in year two, possibly sooner. Saves, pays off the car early, uses the AI app for theory, and cuts the fishing trip and possibly the second car.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way he can work with.
S3.quote: In five years, a year of watching is a fifth of it gone.
S3.fieldNote: David's habit of waiting runs up against the shorter timeline, and he notices that himself during the interview. Retraining as a mechanic is a concrete, practical choice. The cost of his plan falls partly on his partner, which he regrets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good news in a way, it's time to sort things out properly. I'd say the same as with the five years, start now, but without the panic. People listen better without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fifty-three and the kids are grown or nearly. I'd have time to get the mechanic's ticket, work a few years with it, and maybe get a bit saved. It still ends with robots doing most of it, but I'd be better off than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the dozer for the first couple of years and get the pay step, then start the mechanic's course once I'd seen how the first lot of retrainees went. I'd get properly comfortable with the AI tools along the way. We'd also put a little into a fund for Freya's studies, because she wants to be a vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the end of the road, but okay about the road itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Freya wanting to be a vet matter in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want her to have a better start than I did. If she can get through a degree before it all lands, she's got something. And I'd like to think a vet still needs hands on a sick dog, even with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start the course sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a couple of the guys came back from it and were doing well. That's how I work. Show me one good result and I'm in.

S4.say: He'd call ten years good news in a way, time to sort things out properly, and urge people to start now without panic.
S4.think: He thinks a decade lets him earn the mechanic's ticket, work with it for a few years and save. It still ends with robots doing most work, but he'd be better off than most.
S4.do: Stays on the dozer for two years to get the pay step, then starts the mechanic's course after seeing how early retrainees fare. Gets comfortable with AI tools and starts a small fund for his daughter's vet studies.
S4.feel: Uneasy about the end, but okay about the path there.
S4.quote: Show me one good result and I'm in.
S4.fieldNote: David's approach is consistent across all five pictures: watch, then follow what's proven. More time lets that approach work. His daughter's ambition to be a vet becomes the focus of his longer-term planning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to watch and learn, and that's how I do everything. What would help is help with the mortgage for a while and a straight answer about which jobs will still be there. And training paid for, so I'm not choosing between a course and groceries.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what a guy like me is good at besides the job. I can fix a fence, I coach Jonas's football team, I can calm down a room. Nobody puts that on a form.

headlineQuote: I can fix a fence, I coach Jonas's football team, I can calm down a room. Nobody puts that on a form.
portrait: David Olsen is a 43-year-old dozer operator at a large open-pit bauxite mine, two and a half years in after fifteen years driving a delivery truck. He and his partner Hanna, a nursing home care worker, have two children and only about forty left over in a good fortnight. He uses an AI app for budgeting and prefers to go second, after others have proved a path works. He is calm in the plateau picture, uneasy in the gradual one, and alarmed by the two-year AGI picture, when he'd consider moving to the city. With more time he plans to become a heavy diesel mechanic and save for his daughter's studies.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to watch others and learn, which is how he approaches everything.
whatWouldHelp: Temporary help with the mortgage, a clear answer about which jobs will remain, and paid training so he doesn't have to choose between a course and groceries.
